summary: The addition-and-carry mechanism gives correct polynomial values modulo 100,000 for supported cubic inputs. Its historical dates are supported. The input validator can accept higher-degree expressions that match eight sampled points, after which the engine gives the wrong value.

claims.claim: Difference Engine No. 2 was designed in the 1840s and its calculating section was reconstructed in 1991.
claims.how: The About text matches the 1847–1849 design and the Science Museum’s 1991 calculating engine.

sources.title: The engines
sources.says: Difference Engine No. 2 was designed in 1847 to 1849 and uses finite differences and addition. The full engine has 31-digit precision and supports seventh-order differences.

sources.title: A Modern Sequel
sources.says: The Science Museum reconstructed the calculating engine from the original drawings and completed it in 1991; the printer followed later.

claims.claim: Finite differences calculate polynomial values using additions and carries.
claims.how: The actual phases match 128 independently evaluated cubic polynomials over 32 turns each, including wrap and every decimal carry.

claims.claim: The input reader reliably restricts expressions to degree three.
claims.how: It checks only eight consecutive values. x² + (x−1)(x−2)…(x−8) passes at x=1, but the ninth value should be 40,401 while the machine produces 81.

claims.note: Sampling cannot prove an expression’s polynomial degree. Keep this counterexample until the reader checks the expression itself.

simplified: Five decimal digits and third-order differences replace the historical engine’s 31 digits and seventh-order differences. Negative values are displayed modulo 100,000. Accepted inputs must not be assumed valid solely because their first eight values pass the current check.

fixes.what: Check polynomial degree from the parsed expression, allowing integer-valued polynomials such as n(n+1)/2, and reject unsupported functions or high-degree terms.
